162.content: The tag system allows you to group eggs together by type. This is the successor to nests.

163.content:
Pterodactyl grouped eggs into nests, and each egg belonged to exactly one nest. Pelican replaces nests with tags: an egg can have any number of tags, and tags don't need to be created first.
When migrating from Pterodactyl, each egg gets a tag with the name of its old nest. Locations work the same way for nodes.

165.content: Every egg has a Docker image or Yolk as they are referred to. Images can be custom-made, and you can learn how to create them in the "Creating a Custom Yolk" guide or you can use the pre-made ones found here Yolk Repo. They have two fields that need to be defined: the name of the image and the URL where the image is hosted.

166.content: This is perhaps the most important step in egg configuration, as this tells Wings how to run everything.

167.content: The first field you'll encounter is `Copy Settings From`. The default selection is `None`. That is expected, and okay. This dropdown is discussed at the end of this article.

168.content: Next, you'll encounter `Stop Command` and, as the name implies, this should be the command used to safely stop the server. For some games, this is `stop` or `end`. Certain programs and games don't have a specified stop command, so you can enter `^C`, `^SIGINT`, `^SIGABRT`, `^SIGTERM` or `^SIGKILL` to have Wings end the process.

169.content: Logs are completely handled by Wings and use Docker logs to output the complete output from the server. This can be set like below:

170.content: The next block is one of the most complex blocks, the `Configuration Files` descriptor. Wings will process this block prior to booting the server to ensure all of the required settings are defined and set correctly.

171.content: In this example, we are telling Wings to read `server.properties` in `/home/container`. Within this block, we define a `parser`, in this case `properties` but the following are valid parsers:

172.content: `file` — This parser goes based on matching the beginning of lines, and not a specific property like the other five. Avoid using this parser if possible.

179.content: Once you have defined a parser, we then define a `find` block which tells Wings what specific elements to find and replace. In this example, we have provided four separate items within the `server.properties` file that we want to find and replace to the assigned values. You can use either an exact value, or define a specific server setting from the server configuration. In this case, we're assigning the default server port to be used as the `server.port` and `query.port`. **These placeholders are case sensitive, and should have no spaces in them.**

180.content: You can have multiple files listed here, Wings will process them in parallel before starting the server. When using `yaml` or `json` you can use more advanced searching for elements.

181.content: In this example, we are parsing `config.yml` using the `yaml` parser. The first three find items are simply assigning ports and IPs for the first listener block. The last one, `servers.*.address` uses wildcard matching to match any items within the `servers` block, and then finding each `address` block for those items.

182.content: An advanced feature of this file configuration is the ability to define multiple find and replace statements for a single matching line. In this case, we are looking for either `127.0.0.1` or `localhost` and replacing them with the docker interface defined in the configuration file using `{{config.docker.interface}}`.

183.content: The last block to configure is the `Start Configuration` for servers running using this egg.

184.content: In the example block above, we define `done` as the entire line, or part of a line that indicates a server is done starting, and is ready for players to join. When Wings sees this output, it will mark the server as `RUNNING` rather than `STARTING`.

186.content: As mentioned above, there is a unique `Copy Settings From` dropdown when adding a new egg. This is used in two different places, there is one for the Process Management and one for the Install Script. This gives you the ability to, as the name suggests, copy settings defined above from a different egg.

188.content: One of the great parts of Egg Variables is the ability to define specific variables that users and/or admins can control to tweak different settings without letting users modify the startup command. To create new variables, or edit existing ones, visit the egg you created, and click the `Variables` tab at the top of the page. Let's take a look at an example variable that we can create.

189.content: The name and description are rather self-explanatory, so I'll skip down to the `Environment Variable` box. This should be an alphanumeric name with underscores, and should be uppercase. This will be the name of the environment variable which can be accessed in the startup command as `{{WOOZLE_WOO}}`, within file modifications as `{{server.environment.WOOZLE_WOO}}`, or just `${WOOZLE_WOO}` in any shell scripts (it is passed through in the environment). We also define a default value for this environment variable in this example, but it is not required to do so.

190.content: Egg variables can be referenced in three different ways depending on the context:

194.content: The next section is `Permissions`, which is a dropdown with two options: `Users Can View` and `Users Can Edit`.

195.content: `Users Can View` — allows a user to view the field on the front-end, as well as the assigned value of that variable. They will be able to see it replaced in their startup command.

196.content: `Users Can Edit` — allows a user to edit the value of the variable, for example the name of their `server.jar` file if running Minecraft.

197.content: You should use caution here, even if you assign neither of the permissions it does not mean that the value will be hidden. Crafty users will still be able to get the environment on their server. In most cases this is simply hiding it from the user, and then used within the Dockerfile to perform actions, thus it is not important for the user to see.

198.content: Finally, you will need to define some input rules to validate the value against. In this example, we use `required|string|between:1,10`, which means the field is `required`, must be a `string`, and must be between `1` and `10` characters in length. You can find all of the available validation rules in the Laravel validation documentation. You can also use regex-based validation by using the `regex:` rule flag. For example, `required|regex:/^([\w\d._-]+)(\.jar)$/` will require the field, and will match the regex as any letters or numbers (`\w\d`) including underscore (`_`), periods (`.`), and dashes (`-`) ending in `.jar`.

199.content: They will then be visible when managing the startup for a server in both the Admin CP and on the Front-End.

224.content: Build a custom yolk, a Docker image for Pelican eggs, by writing the Dockerfile and entrypoint script that Wings uses to start servers.

235.content: A yolk is the Docker image an egg runs in. This page builds one: the Dockerfile and the entrypoint script that Wings uses to start a server.

236.content: The most important part of this process is to create the `Dockerfile` that will be used by Wings. Due to heavy restrictions on server containers, you must setup this file in a specific manner.

237.content: In the past we have tried to make use of Alpine Linux as much as possible for our images in order to keep their size down. But for my example we will just use what most eggs are built on, Ubuntu.

238.content: Let's walk through the `Dockerfile` above. The first thing you'll notice is the `FROM` declaration.

239.content: In this case, we are using `eclipse-temurin:8-jdk-noble` which provides us with Java 8.

240.content: The `--platform=$TARGETOS/$TARGETARCH` flag tells Docker which platform architecture to use when pulling the base image.

243.content:
Docker automatically sets these during the build based on your target platform.
This is essential for cross-platform builds and ensuring containers run correctly on different architectures.

244.content: The next thing we do is install the dependencies we will need using Ubuntu's package manager: `apt-get`. To keep things clean everything is being contained in a single `RUN` block.

245.content: Within this `RUN` block, you'll notice the `useradd` command. This is needed to be sure the container has the correct permissions within the system.

246.content: After we create that user, we then define the default container `USER` as well as a few `ENV` settings to be applied to things running within the container.

247.content: One of the last things we do is define a `WORKDIR` which is where everything else will be executed. The `WORKDIR` must be set to `/home/container`.

248.content: Finally, we need to copy our `ENTRYPOINT` script into the docker image root. This is done using `COPY`, after which we define the command to be used when the container is started using `CMD`. The `CMD` line should always point to the `entrypoint.sh` file.

249.content: The `ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/tini", "-g", "--"]` line sets up Tini as the init process for the container.

250.content: **What is Tini:** Tini is a minimal init system that acts as PID 1 inside the container, handling process signals and reaping zombie processes.

252.content: `-g` - Sends signals to the entire process group, not just the child process

253.content: `--` - Separates Tini's arguments from the command that follows

255.content: **Signal handling:** Ensures signals (like `SIGTERM` during container shutdown) are properly forwarded to your application, allowing graceful shutdowns

256.content: **Zombie reaping:** Prevents zombie processes from accumulating when child processes aren't properly cleaned up

257.content: In order to complete this `Dockerfile`, we will need an `entrypoint.sh` file which tells Docker how to run this specific server type.

258.content: These entrypoint files are actually fairly abstracted, and Wings will pass in the start command as an environment variable before processing it and then executing the command.

259.content: The second command, `cd /home/container`, simply ensures we are in the correct directory when running the rest of the commands. We then follow that up with `java -version` to output this information to end-users, but that is not necessary.

260.content: The most significant part of this file is the `MODIFIED_STARTUP` environment variable. What we are doing in this case is parsing the environment `STARTUP` that is passed into the container by Wings. In most cases, this variable looks something like the example below:

261.content: You'll notice some placeholders there, specifically `{{SERVER_MEMORY}}` and `{{SERVER_JARFILE}}`. These both refer to other environment variables being passed in, and they look something like the example below.

262.content: There are a host of different environment variables, and they change depending on the specific egg configuration. However, that is not necessarily anything to worry about here.

263.content: The command above simply evaluates the `STARTUP` environment variable, and then replaces anything surrounded in curly braces `{{EXAMPLE}}` with a matching environment variable (such as `EXAMPLE`). Thus, our `STARTUP` command:

265.content: The last step is to run this modified startup command, which is done with the line `${MODIFIED_STARTUP}`.

287.content: Some cloud images leave out kernel modules Docker needs:

288.content: On **CentOS Stream, AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux 10**, `xt_addrtype` is missing, so Docker installs but won't start.

291.content: If `sudo modprobe xt_addrtype` (or `xt_ipvs`) still can't find the module, the package was installed for a newer kernel than the one running: reboot and try again. The install script does all of this for you.

292.content: If none of this works on your server, see the official Docker documentation on how to install Docker CE.

293.content: If you are on an operating system with systemd (Ubuntu 16+, Debian 8+, CentOS 7+) run the command below to have Docker start when you boot your machine.

294.content: On most systems, Docker will be unable to setup swap space by default. You can confirm this by running `docker info` and looking for the output of `WARNING: No swap limit support` near the bottom.

295.content: Enabling swap is entirely optional, but we recommended doing it if you will be hosting for others and to prevent OOM errors.

296.content:
To enable swap, open `/etc/default/grub` as a root user and find the line starting with `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT`. Make
sure the line includes `swapaccount=1` somewhere inside the double-quotes.

297.content:
After that, run `sudo update-grub` followed by `sudo reboot` to restart the server and have swap enabled.
Below is an example of what the line should look like, _do not copy this line verbatim. It often has additional OS-specific parameters._

298.content:
Some Linux distros may ignore `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT`.  
Therefore you might have to use `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX` instead should the above variable not work for you.

308.content:
An AI assistant (ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor and the like) can walk you through an install, explain each command and read your error messages with you.

309.content:
Assistants make mistakes, and they often mix Pelican up with Pterodactyl, which it was forked from: other paths, commands and versions.
**Read every command before you run it**, and never paste passwords, API keys, tokens or your `APP_KEY` into a chat.
Try a new install on a fresh server or a snapshot first.

501.content: Mounts is a feature that allows administrators to mount other directories from the host file-system into a Server's container.

502.content: For security reasons it is not possible to mount directories on a node by default.

503.content: **Directories that should be mountable have to be specified explicitly in the Wings configuration.**

504.content: In the Wings configuration file (`/etc/pelican/config.yml`) the `allowed_mounts` field is used to list mountable directories. The listed directories and all their subdirectories can be mounted.

505.content: You have to restart Wings to apply new changes to your Wings config.

602.content: Help translate the Pelican Panel on Crowdin, including how approval works, how to handle placeholders and plurals and how to request a new language.

609.content:
The Panel is translated by the community on Crowdin. Anyone can help, no coding needed.
There is no minimum a language has to reach: whatever is translated ships, and missing strings fall back to English.

610.content: This covers translating the Panel itself. The documentation site is only available in English.

611.content: Create a Crowdin account and join the pelican-dev project.

612.content: Pick your language and start translating strings in the Crowdin editor.

613.content:
Please do **not** open pull requests that change files in `lang/` by hand. Translations are synced from Crowdin automatically and manual changes get overwritten.
The English source strings live in `lang/en/**/*.php` in the panel repository. If you add new strings in a code contribution, add them to `lang/en` only.

614.content: Only **approved** translations are shipped. Proofreaders review suggested translations for their language and approve them.

615.content: If your language has no proofreader, or you want to become one, ask in the Crowdin project discussions or on our Discord.

616.content: Keep placeholders exactly as they are in the English string.

617.content: **Placeholders** start with a `:` and get replaced with a value. Don't translate or remove them, but you can move them around in the sentence.

618.content: **Plurals** are separated by `|`. In English the first part is the singular and the second the plural. Use as many forms as your language needs, in the order your language's plural rules expect. Explicit ranges like `{0} No files|[1,*] :count files` work too.

619.content: Keep HTML tags like `<b>` as they are, only translate the text between them.

620.content: Ask for the language to be added in the Crowdin project. Once it has approved strings it shows up in the Panel with the next sync.

621.content: Most languages need no code changes. Only languages with a regional code need a mapping in `crowdin.yml` (`languages_mapping`), for example `zh-CN` → `zh_CN` and `pt-BR` → `pt_BR`.

622.content: Two GitHub workflows in the panel repository keep Crowdin and the code in sync:

623.content: **Upload Crowdin Sources** (`upload-sources.yml`) runs on every push to `main` that changes `lang/en/**` or `crowdin.yml`, and uploads the English strings to Crowdin.

624.content: **Download Crowdin Translations** (`download-translations.yml`) runs every Sunday at 00:00 UTC (and can be started manually). It downloads all approved translations, formats them with Pint and opens a "New Crowdin Translations" pull request from the `i18n_crowdin_translations` branch.

625.content: After that pull request is merged, the translations are part of the next release.

626.content:
Every language folder in `lang/` can be selected on the user's profile page, plus languages provided by plugins.
Languages other than English show a note that they may not be fully translated, with an "Update On Crowdin" link back to the project.
Any string that isn't translated yet is shown in English.

628.content: Diagnose common Pelican problems: panel 500 errors and logs, Wings connection issues, schedules not running, file uploads and plugin removal.

642.content: Start here when something in Pelican doesn't work. This page shows where to find the Panel's logs and how to fix common Panel errors, Wings connection problems, schedules that don't run, failing file uploads and plugins that won't uninstall.

643.content: If you see a `500 | SERVER ERROR` or `An unexpected error was encountered while processing this request` you have to check your panel logs by running the following command.

645.content: `ErrorException: file_put_contents(_____): failed to open stream: Permission denied`: Wrong file permissions/ ownership for the panel files, see below.

646.content: `502 Bad Gateway Error`: Make sure that php-fpm is running and that you are using the correct php version in your webserver config.

647.content: `CSRF token mismatch`: Enable SSL for your Panel with HTTPS protocol scheme in the `APP_URL`, or set `SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE` to `false` in your `.env` file.

648.content: `Connection refused [tcp://_______:6379]`: Redis isn't running or isn't reachable for some other reason. (start by checking the status of the redis service: `systemctl status redis-server`)

649.content: `SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name '_______'`: The used SSL certificate for your panel isn't valid for your panel domain, see this guide for creating a new SSL certificate.

650.content: `General error: 8 attempt to write a readonly database`: Your `database.sqlite` has wrong file permissions and is read-only. Make sure the file is writable and owned by the correct user.

651.content: `Class '_____' not found`: This usually means you are missing php extensions. Make sure all needed extensions are installed and that you are using the correct php version.

652.content: `Connection timed out after 5001 milliseconds for _______:8080`: Your panel can't reach wings, see the wings connection issues steps below.

653.content:
If the command above doesn't return anything, you most likely have incorrect file permissions . So you first need to fix that.  
You can set the correct permissions by running `sudo chmod -R 755 /var/www/pelican/storage/* /var/www/pelican/bootstrap/cache/`. Also make sure that your panel files are owned by the correct user.

654.content:
First you should make sure that the wings service is running. To do that run `systemctl status wings`.  
It should say that the service is active and running. If its in a failed state run `sudo wings diagnostics` to check the wings logs for errors.

656.content: `open /etc/letsencrypt/live/_____________/fullchain.pem: no such file or directory`: The SSL certificate for wings is missing, see this guide for creating a SSL certificate.

657.content: `Pool overlaps with other one on this address space`: You already have a docker network using the default subnet. (`172.18.0.0/16`) Change the subnet in your wings config file and use `systemctl stop wings && docker network rm pelican_nw && systemctl start wings` to apply the change.

658.content: `Error response from Panel: AccessDeniedHttpException: You are not authorized to access this resource. (HTTP/403)`: Your wings token is wrong, you need update the token in your config.yml file

659.content: `Error response from Panel: _MissingResponseCode: No error response returned from API endpoint`: Your panel is not responding correctly. This usually happens when Cloudflare is blocking the connection. In that case make sure your wings ip is added to the Cloudflare firewall. If you aren't using Cloudflare it might be some other CDN/ DDoS protection service or your provider.

660.content: `remote: could not unmarshal response: invalid character '<' looking for beginning of value`: This is basically the same error as above: Cloudflare is blocking the connection.

661.content:
If you confirmed that wings is running without errors you should make sure that the wings port (`8080` by default) isn't blocked by any firewall. The best way to check this is to use online port checkers like dnschecker.org  
It should say "open" if you check for your node FQDN (e.g. `node.example.com` or `123.123.123.123`) and your wings port (e.g. `8080`). If it says "timed-out" you have some firewall blocking the port. This could be an internal firewall (like iptables) or an external firewall (e.g. from your provider).

662.content:
If your panel and wings are on the same machine or same network, and you are using domains you should check for NAT loop back issues.  
Edit the `/etc/hosts` file on your panel/ wings machine and add an entry for your ip and domain.

If the connection checks above were both successfull you might have misconfigured the Node settings in the Panel.  
Make sure that your Node FQDN/ IP, Port and Scheme (HTTP/ HTTPS) is correct.

When using a reverse proxy you might have different external and internal ports for Wings. (e.g. `80` internally and `443` externally)  
In that case make sure the Node settings in the Panel uses the external port while the Wings config file uses the internal port!

672.content: If your Schedules are stuck on `Processing` or don't execute the tasks check the following:

673.content: Is your Schedule set to run `ONLY WHEN SERVER IS ONLINE` and the server is currently offline?

674.content: Is your queue worker service running? (`systemctl status pelican-queue`)

675.content: Is your queue worker service using the correct PHP version? (`php -v`)

676.content:
Is your cronjob setup correctly? `crontab -l -u www-data` (where `www-data` is your webserver user) should show the following entry:  
`* * * * * php /var/www/pelican/artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1`

677.content: If your queue worker service is not running you can also check the panel logs for errors.

678.content: To recreate the queue worker service you can run `php /var/www/pelican/artisan p:environment:queue-service --overwrite`.

679.content: If a file upload form returns an error like `mountedActionsData.0.files.24d4b82d-a3ae-47fd-981f-8b2f0f6a21d4` it is most likely a proxy issue.

680.content:
Make sure your `Trusted Proxies` are set to the correct ips, both in the panel settings and your proxy settings!  
Also make sure your webserver and/ or proxy have a high enough upload limit. (e.g. `client_max_body_size`, `upload_max_filesize` and `post_max_size`)

681.content: In some cases the issue can also be caused by incorrect file permissions. See above on how to fix your file permissions.

682.content:
If you can't uninstall a plugin via the admin panel, you may have to do it via ssh.

817.content: A Cloudflare Tunnel lets you serve the panel over HTTPS without opening any inbound ports on your host. A small `cloudflared` container makes an outbound connection to Cloudflare, and Cloudflare forwards requests for your hostname down that connection to the panel.

822.content: Open the Cloudflare dashboard and go to **Networking** → **Tunnels**. (In the older Zero Trust dashboard this is **Networks** → **Tunnels**.)

823.content: Click **Create a tunnel**, choose **Cloudflared**, give it a name (e.g. `pelican`) and save it.

824.content: On the install screen, copy the token from the shown command (the long string after `--token`). You do not need to install anything on the host, Docker will run `cloudflared` for you.

825.content: Under **Routes**, click **Add route** and choose **Published application** (called a public hostname in older versions of the dashboard):

826.content: **Subdomain** and **Domain**: the hostname you want the panel on, e.g. `panel.example.com`

829.content: `panel:80` is the panel container's name and internal port. Cloudflare creates the DNS record for the hostname automatically.

830.content: Create a directory for the panel, and in it a `.env` file holding your tunnel token. Docker Compose reads this file automatically, which keeps the token out of `compose.yml`.

832.content: Compared to the standard Docker setup:

833.content: There is no `ports:` section. Nothing is published on the host, all traffic arrives through the tunnel.

834.content: `APP_URL` is the public `https://` hostname from the tunnel.

835.content: `BEHIND_PROXY` makes the panel listen on plain HTTP port 80 and skip Let's Encrypt, since Cloudflare handles TLS (SSL). See Reverse Proxy Configuration.

836.content: `TRUSTED_PROXIES` is the Docker network's subnet, so the panel trusts the forwarded headers from the `cloudflared` container. If you change the subnet, change both.

838.content: You should see `Registered tunnel connection`, and the tunnel should show as **Healthy** in the Cloudflare dashboard.

839.content: Now back up your encryption key and open `https://panel.example.com/installer` to finish installing.

840.content: Wings cannot share the panel's tunnel hostname. The panel talks to Wings, and your users' browsers open a websocket directly to Wings for the console, so the node's FQDN must be reachable on its own. You can either:

841.content: Expose Wings directly, optionally through the Cloudflare proxy. See Enabling Cloudflare proxy.

842.content: Route a second public hostname on a tunnel to Wings. When creating the node, choose **HTTPS with (reverse) proxy**, which sets the connection port to `443` and the listen port to `8080`, and point the tunnel's service at `http://<wings host>:8080`.

844.content: SFTP (port `2022` by default) is plain TCP and does not work through an HTTP tunnel. Expose it directly if you need it.

845.content: Cloudflare limits request body size by plan (100 MB on Free and Pro). Uploads through a proxied Wings hostname larger than that will fail.

846.content: Run Wings in its own compose project rather than adding it to this one, so a not-yet-configured Wings does not restart in a loop alongside the panel.

847.content: **The tunnel is healthy but the site returns a 502 or "Unable to reach origin service"**

848.content: Check the public hostname's URL is `panel:80` (not `localhost:80`) and the type is `HTTP`.

849.content: Check the panel container is running with `docker compose ps`. On first start, it may still be applying migrations, see `docker compose logs panel`.

850.content: **The site redirects in a loop, or the panel exits complaining about a Let's Encrypt email**

852.content: **Pages load but links, assets or logins use the wrong address**

853.content: `APP_URL` must match the tunnel hostname exactly, including `https://`.

855.content: `TRUSTED_PROXIES` must cover the subnet the `cloudflared` container is on.

856.content: Do not commit `.env`. Anyone with the tunnel token can run your tunnel.

1303.content: How Pelican versions the Panel and Wings with semantic versioning, what counts as a breaking change, and how deprecations, releases and support work.

1315.content:
The Panel and Wings are versioned **independently**. A Panel release does not mean there is a Wings release with the same number, and the other way around.
Compatibility is guaranteed within a major version: any Panel `1.x` works with any Wings `1.x` at or above the Panel's minimum Wings version.
See Updating the Panel and Updating Wings for the current requirements.

1317.content: The minimum Wings version is only raised in a **minor** Panel release and is announced in the release notes.

1318.content: The Panel checks the Wings version of every node and shows two kinds of warnings:

1319.content: **Outdated**: the node runs an older Wings than the latest release. It still works, but you should update Wings.

1320.content: **Incompatible**: the node runs a Wings older than the Panel's minimum. The node icon turns yellow, the node page shows the required version and the health check fails. Update Wings as soon as possible.

1321.content: The Panel never blocks a node because of its Wings version. An incompatible node keeps working, but features that need a newer Wings may fail.
